>MDL (programming language)

>Developer MIT Project MAC

>Typing discipline: Dynamic, strong
>Scope: Static, lexical
>Implementation language: MDL
>Platform: PDP-10, VAX, Apollo/Domain
>OS: ITS, TENEX, TOPS-20, BSD, AEGIS
>License: Open-source
>Influenced by: Lisp
>Influenced: ZIL, Planner, Scheme, Common Lisp, Java, Prolog, Smalltalk; actor model, interactive fiction
>MDL (Model Development Language, or colloquially also referred to as More Datatypes than Lisp: or MIT Design Language) is a programming language, a descendant of the language Lisp. Its initial purpose was to provide high level language support for the Dynamic Modeling Group at Massachusetts Institute of Technology's (MIT) Project MAC. It was initially developed in 1971 on a PDP-10 computer on a time-sharing operating system named Incompatible Timesharing System (ITS). It later ran on TENEX, TOPS-20, BSD, and AEGIS.
>The initial development team consisted of Gerald Sussman and Carl Hewitt of the Artificial Intelligence Lab, and Chris Reeve, Bruce Daniels, and David Cressey of the Dynamic Modeling Group. Later, Stu Galley, also of the Dynamic Modeling Group, wrote the MDL documentation.
>MDL was initially called Muddle. This style of self-deprecating humor was not widely understood or appreciated outside of Project MAC and a few other early citadels of information technology. So the name was sanitized to MDL.
>MDL provides several enhancements to classic Lisp. It supports several built-in data types, including lists, strings and arrays, and user-defined data types. It offers multithreaded expression evaluation and coroutines. Variables can carry both a local value within a scope, and a global value, for passing data between scopes. Advanced built-in functions supported interactive debugging of MDL programs, incremental development, and reconstruction of source programs from object programs.
>Although MDL is obsolete, some of its features have been incorporated in later versions of Lisp. Gerald Sussman went on to develop the Scheme language, in collaboration with Guy Steele, who later wrote the specifications for Common Lisp and Java. Carl Hewitt had already published the idea for the language Planner before the MDL project began, but his subsequent thinking on Planner reflected lessons learned from building MDL. Planner concepts influenced languages such as Prolog and Smalltalk. Smalltalk and Simula, in turn, influenced Hewitt's future work on the actor model.
>But the largest influence that MDL had was on the software genre of interactive fiction (IF). An IF game named Zork, sometimes called Dungeon, was first written in MDL. Later, Reeve, Daniels, Galley and other members of Dynamic Modeling went on to start Infocom, a company that produced many early commercial works of interactive fiction.
>In 1980 Marc Blank and Joel Berez adapted the MDL language to create a subset called ZIL (Zork Implementation Language) which was used extensively by Infocom to create their award winning games.

There's already a technology that can do that - magnetohydrodynamic generation [1]. A conductive material moving through a magnetic field develops a voltage across it, which can be used to produce power; a hot plasma is a conductive material with lots of energy that can drive movement.
The problem is that most of the energy produced in fusion is in the kinetic energy of neutrons. To capture that energy, you need to slow the neutrons down by collisions with some material, turning the kinetic energy into heat in that material, and then harvest the heat. AIUI, neutrons being neutral, you need that material to be dense (lots of nuclei per unit volume) and have a high neutron cross-section. The plasma in a fusion reactor is neither, so you can't collect the neutron energy in the plasma. Rather, you have to let the neutrons hit some dense blanket surrounding the plasma, collect the energy as heat there, and then harvest that.
There are fusion reactions which don't produce neutrons [1], and so where the energy goes into the kinetic energy of charged particles, which is readily collected in the plasma, using MHD or direct conversion [3] (is MHD considered a kind of direct conversion?). But they are much harder to do than the reactions which do produce neutrons, and those are already hard enough!

author: dalke
storyTitle: Why I Am Not a Member of the American Psychological Association
text:
Historical examples (polio and TB) that fit your #2 criteria don't seem to have the conflicts that you mention - because the organizations can change focus. Disease research isn't predictable enough to be able to make financial or organizational planning like you propose. Hence, I don't think your worry #2 is realistic. Here's my reasoning.
The March of Dimes started in 1938 as the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis. They started the serious fundraising and research projects for polio, and provided about $233 million on patient care over 20 years, as well as funding research into a cure. They recruited Salk to work on it, which lead to the successful polio vaccine.
The National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis therefore no longer had  a reason to exist. Quoting from http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_of_Dimes#Criticism :
> In his book Essentials of Sociology: A Down-to-Earth Approach, sociologist Professor James M. Henslin describes March of Dimes as a bureaucracy that has taken on a life of its own through a classic example of a process called goal displacement. Faced with redundancy after Jonas Salk discovered the polio vaccine, it adopted a new mission, "fighting birth defects", which was recently changed to a vaguer goal of "breakthrough for babies", rather than disbanding.
You'll note that that they strongly pushed for a true cure. It was only afterwards where they had organization problems. You'll also note that those affected by polio still needed care, so the organization was still useful even after the vaccine.
Similarly, there were a large number of tuberculosis organization. They too changed mission after effective treatments were found. The Saranac Laboratory for the Study of Tuberculosis, for example, became the Trudeau Sanatorium, which then closed when an effective TB treatment was discovered. More famously, the National Association for the Study and Prevention of Tuberculosis, after the TB treatment discovery, became the American Lung Association.
Can you point to real-world examples where was a "true cure" but where organizations pushing for the cure ended up delaying the result, due likely to a conflict of interest with major sponsors? Because the historical record suggests that the organizations are more likely to continue to exist be changing focus, then by suppressing or delaying a cure.
Regarding another aspect of #2, no one knows what a diabetes treatment might be. It could be an expensive treatment. It could take several years for a cure to take effect. It could be a preventative, which only helps those without diabetes but not those who currently have it. It could help one type of diabetes but not another. Some of these are very financially rewarding.
Since members of the ADA almost certainly have friends or relatives who have diabetes, they have a strong emotional reason to want success, independent of money. Since it's impossible to know beforehand if a certain treatment path will be successful, much less the financial possibilities of a successful treatment, it's hard to really game the system that way. Since multiple organizations are working on a cure, it's hard also to game all of the researchers.
Mind you, there's no promise that there is a true cure for diabetes. But there are ways to manage it, hence the terminology.
BTW, I don't know what you mean by "new word." The phrase "diabetes management" dates back to at least the 1970s. Eg, http://diabetes.diabetesjournals.org/content/21/Supplement_2... is a 1972 article titled "Current Unsolved Problems in Diabetes Management", and a literature search finds many other references from that era.
An n-gram search [1] suggests that the preferred phrase was "control of diabetes" until the early 1980s, with "diabetes management" overshadowing it by the mid-1990s.
[1] The n-gram search URL is https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=diabetes+manag...

text:
I agree with nkozyra.
Many people use that quote for something which is NOT "a reasonable argument". It's been so often misused that it has acquired a meaning different than what MLK intended it to mean. As a result, it's almost impossible to use in a reasonable argument, or more strongly, those who can make a reasonable argument on the topic know to not use the quote because it will be willfully misinterpreted.
Consider the Black Lives Matter movement as a concrete example.
"Black Lives Matter" doesn't mean that no other lives matter, "it means that Black lives, which are seen as without value within White supremacy, are important to your liberation. Given the disproportionate impact state violence has on Black lives, we understand that when Black people in this country get free, the benefits will be wide reaching and transformative for society as a whole." - https://www.thefeministwire.com/2014/10/blacklivesmatter-2/
One reaction to BLM is to argue that "All Lives Matter" and that it's wrong to single out blacks. Some of those who make that argument repeat that famous MLK quote.
But as many have pointed out, this is a fundamental misunderstanding of the BLM movement. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Lives_Matter#Criticism for some of the criticism - which I think are valid.
That is, the "All Lives Matter" reaction serves mostly to cover up or ignore the actual systemic and structural racism which have affected black people in the US for centuries.
Again, with a concrete example, until it was prohibited in the 1970s, redlining was used to segregate blacks and whites. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redlining for details. Blacks had higher interest rates, and were often only able to live in poorer parts of town. Until its was prohibited in 1968, covenenta were often used to exclude blacks from the new postwar suburbs. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenant_(law)#Exclusionary_Co... .
As a result, black families in the US generally did not have the same ability to build wealth through home equity that white families did.
Even though those overt practices are now illegal, there are still black people alive who directly suffered from these racially biased laws.
I am convinced that there is a need for reparations, for institutional actions done to people who are still alive. Just like we gave reparations to the Japanese-Americans interned during WWII.
But many oppose any talk of reparations by using that same MLK quote. Because of course any reparations for black people who faced life-long effects of the then-legal racial discrimination must necessarily concern race.
Thus, that MLK quote seems often used as a way to justify ignoring any of the concrete, real-world problems that blacks face.
This is a willful misreading of that quote, because MLK supported reparations - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.#Compens... .
Now, certainly some people use that quote naively, without understanding how it's been re-appropriated. But this means those people also don't have a basic understanding of the issues involved, which means they are not using that quote as "part of a reasonable argument."
FWIW, My experiences is also that most people who use that quote do so from cherry picking. They don't agree with most of the rest of MLK's views, like reparations (above) or his view that "There must be a better distribution of wealth, and maybe America must move toward a democratic socialism", or his anti-war "Beyond Vietnam" speech.

In the sociology of science, "Matthew effect" was a term coined by Robert K. Merton to describe how, among other things, eminent scientists will often get more credit than a comparatively unknown researcher, even if their work is similar; it also means that credit will usually be given to researchers who are already famous.
